claim: RALF1 peptides induce strong repression of main root growth in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: The application of RALF1 peptides induces strong repression of main root growth in Arabidopsis thaliana (Haruta et al., 2014; Figure 1A and B), which we initially used here as a bioassay to visualise RALF1 activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Haruta et al., 2014 and reference to experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B

claim: EGCG is a natural inhibitor of PME activity.
source: EGCG is a natural inhibitor of PME activity (Lewis et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2008

claim: Epicatechin (EC) is not an inhibitor of PMEs.
source: In contrast, the structurally similar epicatechin (EC) is not an inhibitor of PMEs (Lewis et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lewis et al., 2008

claim: EC did not block RALF1-induced root growth repression.
source: In contrast, the structurally similar epicatechin (EC) is not an inhibitor of PMEs (Lewis et al., 2008) and did not block RALF1-induced root growth repression (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: EGCG but not EC application reduced the labelling of de-methyl esterified pectin in roots.
source: In agreement, EGCG but not EC application reduced the labelling of de-methyl esterified pectin in roots (Figure 1E and F) as visualised by the fluorescent probe COS488 (Mravec et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and F and citation to Mravec et al., 2014 for the probe

claim: PMEI3 overexpression interferes with PME activity.
source: To consolidate this assumption, we employed the overexpression of PECTIN METHYLESTERASE INHIBITOR 3 (PMEI3), which is well characterised to interfere with PME activity (Peaucelle et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citations to Peaucelle et al., 2008 and Xu et al., 2022

claim: PMEI3 overexpression reduced the extracellular de-methylesterification of pectin in epidermal root cells.
source: To consolidate this assumption, we employed the overexpression of PECTIN METHYLESTERASE INHIBITOR 3 (PMEI3), which is well characterised to interfere with PME activity (Peaucelle et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2022) and accordingly also reduced the extracellular de-methylesterification of pectin in epidermal root cells (Figure 1G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and H

claim: PMEI3 and PMEI5 gain-of-function reduced the RALF1-induced root growth repression.
source: In agreement with the EGCG application, PMEI3, as well as PMEI5, gain-of-function reduced the RALF1-induced root growth repression (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I and J

claim: Pharmacological and genetic interference with PME activity leads to the repression of RALF1 effects on root growth.
source: We accordingly conclude that pharmacological and genetic interference with PME activity leads to the repression of RALF1 effects on root growth.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of EGCG and PMEI experiments

claim: The flg22 peptide is derived from the N-terminus of bacterial flagellin and is known to elicit root growth repression via the innate immune receptor flagellin sensitive2 (FLS2).
source: The flg22 peptide is derived from the N-terminus of bacterial flagellin and is known to elicit root growth repression via the innate immune receptor flagellin sensitive2 (FLS2) (Chinchilla et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chinchilla et al., 2007

claim: EGCG treatments were not able to suppress, but instead additively enhanced the FLG22-induced root growth repression.
source: EGCG treatments were not able to suppress, but instead additively enhanced the FLG22-induced root growth repression (Figure 1K and L), suggesting a rather specific effect of PME inhibition on balancing RALF1 activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K and L

claim: PME inhibition has a rather specific effect on balancing RALF1 activity.
source: EGCG treatments were not able to suppress, but instead additively enhanced the FLG22-induced root growth repression (Figure 1K and L), suggesting a rather specific effect of PME inhibition on balancing RALF1 activity.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of EGCG on RALF1 versus flg22 responses

claim: RALF1 induces swollen cell walls as observed by electron microscopy.
source: Using electron microscopy, we indeed observed a RALF1-induced effect on cell wall integrity, showing swollen cell walls, but also revealed plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: RALF1 induces plasma membrane invaginations as observed by electron microscopy.
source: Using electron microscopy, we indeed observed a RALF1-induced effect on cell wall integrity, showing swollen cell walls, but also revealed plasma membrane invaginations (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2A and B

claim: RALF1-induced plasma membrane invaginations were confirmed using live cell confocal imaging.
source: These pronounced RALF effects were, to our knowledge, never reported and hence we confirmed these effects independently, using live cell confocal imaging. RALF1-induced invaginations of plasma membrane markers, such as Low-Temperature inducible protein 6b (LTi6b) (Figure 2C) and Novel Plant SNARE 12 (NPSN12) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), were readily detectable.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: RALF1 induces swelling of the apoplastic signal and additional ectopic accumulations as visualized by propidium iodide staining.
source: Similarly, confocal imaging of propidium iodide (PI)-stained cell walls of wild-type seedlings also depicted the RALF1-induced swelling of the apoplastic signal and revealed additional ectopic accumulations (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2D and F

claim: RALF1-induced alterations in cell wall staining were absent in fer-4 loss-of-function mutants.
source: These RALF1-induced alterations were absent in PI-stained fer-4 loss-of-function mutants (Figure 2E and F), suggesting that FER activation is required for these cellular effects of RALF1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: FER activation is required for RALF1-induced cellular effects on cell walls.
source: These RALF1-induced alterations were absent in PI-stained fer-4 loss-of-function mutants (Figure 2E and F), suggesting that FER activation is required for these cellular effects of RALF1.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of RALF1 effects in fer-4 mutants

claim: Pharmacological interference with PME activity abolished the RALF1-induced alterations in cell wall labelling.
source: The pharmacological (Figure 2G and H) as well as genetic (Figure 2J and K) interference with PME activity abolished the RALF1-induced alterations in cell wall labelling, phenocopying fer-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H

claim: Genetic interference with PME activity abolished the RALF1-induced alterations in cell wall labelling.
source: The pharmacological (Figure 2G and H) as well as genetic (Figure 2J and K) interference with PME activity abolished the RALF1-induced alterations in cell wall labelling, phenocopying fer-4 mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2J and K

claim: PME inhibition phenocopies fer-4 mutants with respect to RALF1-induced cell wall alterations.
source: The pharmacological (Figure 2G and H) as well as genetic (Figure 2J and K) interference with PME activity abolished the RALF1-induced alterations in cell wall labelling, phenocopying fer-4 mutants.
evidence: Inferred from the similar phenotypes of PME inhibition and fer-4 mutants

claim: RALF1 binding to FER leads to rapid apoplastic (extracellular) alkalinisation.
source: On a cellular level, RALF binding to FER leads to rapid apoplastic (extracellular) alkalinisation (Haruta et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Haruta et al., 2014

claim: RALF1 application induced an extracellular pH alkalisation in wild-type epidermal root cells.
source: As expected, the application of RALF1 peptides induced an extracellular pH alkalisation in wild-type epidermal root cells (Barbez et al., 2017; Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B and citation to Barbez et al., 2017

claim: EGCG application abolished the RALF-induced alkalisation of the apoplastic pH.
source: In contrast, EGCG application (Figure 3A and B) as well as the overexpression of PMEI3 (Figure 3C and D), abolished the RALF-induced alkalisation of the apoplastic pH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: PMEI3 overexpression abolished the RALF-induced alkalisation of the apoplastic pH.
source: In contrast, EGCG application (Figure 3A and B) as well as the overexpression of PMEI3 (Figure 3C and D), abolished the RALF-induced alkalisation of the apoplastic pH.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and D

claim: Interference with PME activity disrupts the primary output signalling of RALF1 in root cells.
source: We accordingly conclude that interference with PME activity disrupts the primary output signalling of RALF1 in root cells.
evidence: Inferred from the abolishment of RALF1-induced pH alkalisation by PME inhibition

claim: RALF1 induces ligand-induced endocytosis of FER.
source: Therefore, we next tested whether the RALF1 ligand-induced endocytosis of FER is altered upon changes in the methylation status of pectin. In agreement with previous reports, we observed the RALF1-induced internalisation of functional FER::FER-GFP in epidermal root cells (Figure 3F and G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and G

claim: Ligand-induced internalisation of FER-GFP was abolished when PME activity was pharmacologically suppressed.
source: On the other hand, the ligand-induced internalisation of FER-GFP was abolished when we pharmacologically or genetically suppressed PME activity (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–J

claim: Ligand-induced internalisation of FER-GFP was abolished when PME activity was genetically suppressed.
source: On the other hand, the ligand-induced internalisation of FER-GFP was abolished when we pharmacologically or genetically suppressed PME activity (Figure 3F–J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F–J

claim: PME activity is required for the earliest events of RALF1 perception by FER in roots.
source: These findings propose that the PME activity is required for the earliest events of RALF1 perception by FER in roots.
evidence: Inferred from the abolishment of FER endocytosis by PME inhibition

claim: RALF34 is a ligand of CrRLK1L theseus1 (THE1).
source: To test the specificity of this observation, we used another RALF peptide called RALF34, which is a ligand of CrRLK1L theseus1 (THE1) (Gonneau et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gonneau et al., 2018

claim: RALF34 application induced the internalisation of FER-GFP.
source: Similar to RALF1, the application of RALF34 induced the internalisation of FER-GFP, which was fully suppressed when PME activity was inhibited (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: RALF34-induced internalisation of FER-GFP was fully suppressed when PME activity was inhibited.
source: Similar to RALF1, the application of RALF34 induced the internalisation of FER-GFP, which was fully suppressed when PME activity was inhibited (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Several RALF peptides display the same or similar signalling modalities.
source: Therefore, we assume that several RALF peptides display the same or similar signalling modalities.
evidence: Inferred from the similar behavior of RALF1 and RALF34

claim: RALF peptides are positively charged.
source: RALF peptides are positively charged (Abarca et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abarca et al., 2021

claim: The association of positively charged RALF1 peptides with de-methylesterified, negatively charged pectin is required for its FER-dependent perception.
source: Hence, it is hence conceivable that the association of positively charged RALF1 peptides with de-methylesterified, negatively charged pectin is required for its FER-dependent perception.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on charge complementarity

claim: High levels of free, de-methylesterified OGs in the media did not visibly affect the cell wall or FER endocytosis on its own.
source: We initially assessed potential OG binding to RALF1, using the RALF1 impact on root cells as a bio-assay. The addition of high levels of free, de-methylesterified OGs into the media did not visibly affect the cell wall or FER endocytosis on its own (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: Free OGs in the medium strongly interfered with RALF1-induced cell wall swelling and FER receptor endocytosis in roots.
source: On the other hand, free OGs in the medium strongly interfered with RALF1-induced cell wall swelling and FER receptor endocytosis in roots (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: The effect of OGs on RALF1 activity was concentration-dependent.
source: This effect was concentration-dependent (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that excess of de-methylesterified OGs in the medium can bind and out-titrate RALF1 peptides and thereby limit the RALF1 activity at the root surface.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: Excess of de-methylesterified OGs in the medium can bind and out-titrate RALF1 peptides and thereby limit the RALF1 activity at the root surface.
source: This effect was concentration-dependent (Figure 4A and B), suggesting that excess of de-methylesterified OGs in the medium can bind and out-titrate RALF1 peptides and thereby limit the RALF1 activity at the root surface.
evidence: Inferred from the concentration-dependent inhibition of RALF1 activity by OGs

claim: RALF1 binds to OG25-50 with an equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) of 105 nM.
source: Biolayer interferometry assays showed the binding between RALF1 and OG25-50 with an Equilibrium dissociation constant (Kd) of 105 nM (C).
evidence: Supported by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 4C

claim: The association and dissociation constants of RALF1-OG binding imply high avidity binding.
source: The association and dissociation constants (kON = 1.02 × 103 M-1 s-1, kOFF _=1.07 × 10–4 s-1) imply high avidity binding (D).
evidence: Supported by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 4D

claim: RALF1 peptides and de-methylesterified OGs undergo low affinity but high avidity binding assemblies.
source: This is indicative of relatively low affinity at the individual RALF1-OG binding event level but multiple intermolecular binding events may eventually lead to a high accumulative binding strength. We hence propose that RALF1 peptides and de-methylesterified OGs undergo low affinity but high avidity binding assemblies.
evidence: Inferred from the kinetic parameters of RALF1-OG binding

claim: The binding of RALF peptides and de-methylesterified OGs leads to phase separation in vitro.
source: This finding complements recent data, indicating that the binding of RALF peptides and de-methylesterified OGs leads to phase separation in vitro (Liu et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2024

claim: RALF1 contains in total eight positively charged amino acids (three lysine (K) and five arginine (R)).
source: RALF1 contains in total eight positively charged amino acids (three lysine (K) and five arginine (R)) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: Supported by amino acid sequence analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B

claim: PGIP binds to de-methylesterified pectin through a positively charged binding site formed by clustered residues of lysine (K) and arginine (R).
source: This is reminiscent of the well-characterised de-methylesterified pectin-binding protein polygalacturonase-inhibiting protein (PGIP), which binds to de-methylesterified pectin through a positively charged binding site formed by clustered residues of lysine (K) and arginine (R) (Spadoni et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spadoni et al., 2006

claim: The LRX8-RALF4 complex binds de-methylesterified OGs in a charge-dependent manner in pollen.
source: Notably, the LRX8-RALF4 complex binds de-methylesterified OGs in a charge-dependent manner in pollen (Moussu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moussu et al., 2023

claim: RALF1-KR peptides are not bioactive in roots.
source: RALF1-KR peptides are not bioactive, because they did neither affect root growth, nor cell wall integrity, nor did they induce the ligand-induced endocytosis of FER in epidermal root cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–I

claim: The positively charged residues in RALF1 are essential for its activity in roots.
source: These findings suggest that the positively charged residues in RALF1 are essential for its activity in roots.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of bioactivity of RALF1-KR

claim: RALF1-KR does not bind to de-methylesterified OGs.
source: Using our in vitro system, we did not observe RALF1-KR binding to de-methylesterified OGs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J), proposing that RALF1 and OGs indeed interact in a charge-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by biolayer interferometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2J

claim: RALF1 and OGs interact in a charge-dependent manner.
source: Using our in vitro system, we did not observe RALF1-KR binding to de-methylesterified OGs (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J), proposing that RALF1 and OGs indeed interact in a charge-dependent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of binding between RALF1-KR and OGs

claim: The LRX-RALF complex and its interaction with pectin exert a condensing effect on the cell wall in pollen and root hairs.
source: The LRX-RALF complex and its interaction with pectin exert a condensing effect on the cell wall in pollen and root hairs (Moussu et al., 2023; Schoenaers et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moussu et al., 2023 and Schoenaers et al., 2024

claim: LRX proteins bind and link FER with a cell wall-sensing mechanism in roots.
source: Moreover, LRX proteins also bind and link FER with a cell wall-sensing mechanism in roots (Dünser et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dünser et al., 2019

claim: LRX function in root growth appears to be independent of FER-dependent RALF signalling.
source: Nevertheless, LRX function in root growth appears to be independent of FER-dependent RALF signalling (Dünser et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dünser et al., 2019

claim: RALF1 applications induced cell wall alterations in lrx1 lrx2 lrx3 lrx4 lrx5 quintuple mutant roots.
source: We observed that RALF1 applications still induced cell wall alterations in lrx1 lrx2 lrx3 lrx4 lrx5 quintuple mutant roots (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–D

claim: Pharmacological interference with PME activity repressed RALF1 activity in the lrx1 lrx2 lrx3 lrx4 lrx5 quintuple mutant roots.
source: Similar to wild-type roots (Figure 5E and F), pharmacological interference with PME activity still repressed RALF1 activity in the lrx1 lrx2 lrx3 lrx4 lrx5 quintuple mutant roots (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G and H

claim: LRX proteins are not essential for the RALF activity in roots.
source: These findings confirm our previous assumptions that LRX proteins are not essential for the RALF activity in roots (Dünser et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Dünser et al., 2019 and current experimental data

claim: LRX proteins are not required for the PME-dependent control of RALF1 signalling in roots.
source: These findings confirm our previous assumptions that LRX proteins are not essential for the RALF activity in roots (Dünser et al., 2019) and, moreover, reveal that LRX proteins are also not required for the PME-dependent control of RALF1 signalling in roots.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of PME-dependent RALF1 regulation in lrx quintuple mutants

claim: Exogenous application of RALF1 induces prominent plasma membrane protrusions into root epidermal cells.
source: Intriguingly, the exogenous application of RALF1 does not only affect cell wall characteristics but also induces prominent plasma membrane protrusions into root epidermal cells.
evidence: Inferred from the electron microscopy and confocal imaging data

claim: Pharmacological and genetic interference with PME activity specifically abolishes RALF1, but not flg22 peptide, activity in roots.
source: We illustrate that the pharmacological and genetic interference with PME activity specifically abolishes RALF1, but not flg22 peptide, activity in roots.
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing RALF1 and flg22 responses

claim: PME activity is required for all hallmarks of RALF1 signalling, including the rapid alkalinisation of the cell wall and the ligand-induced endocytosis of FER.
source: We conclude that PME activity is required for all hallmarks of RALF1 signalling, including the rapid alkalinisation of the cell wall and the ligand-induced endocytosis of FER.
evidence: Inferred from the comprehensive effects of PME inhibition on RALF1 responses

claim: The generation of de-methylesterified, negatively charged pectin in the cell wall is required for the FER-dependent perception of positively charged RALF1 at the root cell surface.
source: We hence propose that the generation of de-methylesterified, negatively charged pectin in the cell wall is required for the FER-dependent perception of positively charged RALF1 at the root cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of PME inhibition, OG titration, and charge-dependent binding experiments

claim: RALF1 binds in a charge-dependent manner to de-methylesterified OGs in vitro.
source: We show that RALF1 binds in a charge-dependent manner to de-methylesterified OGs in vitro and that the application of free OGs can out-titrate RALF1 peptides in the medium.
evidence: Supported by biolayer interferometry and biological assay data

claim: The application of free OGs can out-titrate RALF1 peptides in the medium.
source: We show that RALF1 binds in a charge-dependent manner to de-methylesterified OGs in vitro and that the application of free OGs can out-titrate RALF1 peptides in the medium.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing concentration-dependent inhibition

claim: The LRX8-RALF4 complex and its charge-dependent binding of de-methylesterified OGs controls extracellular condensations in pollen tubes.
source: In agreement, after we pre-printed a previous version of this manuscript (Rößling et al., 2023), Moussu and colleagues proposed that the LRX8-RALF4 complex and its charge-dependent binding of de-methylesterified OGs controls extracellular condensations in pollen tubes (Moussu et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Moussu et al., 2023

claim: A similar structural mechanism defines root hair growth in a FER-dependent manner.
source: The contribution of FER signalling remains unknown in this process, but a similar structural mechanism defines root hair growth in a FER-dependent manner (Schoenaers et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schoenaers et al., 2024

claim: RALF peptide binding to de-methylesterified pectin is sufficient to lead to its extracellular phase separation, subsequently inducing the clustering of FER receptors in the plasma membrane.
source: Within the main root, the RALF peptide binding to de-methylesterified pectin was suggested to be sufficient to lead to its extracellular phase separation, subsequently inducing the clustering of FER receptors in the plasma membrane (Liu et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2024

claim: LRX proteins directly interact with FER and thereby contribute to cell wall sensing in roots.
source: LRX proteins directly interact with FER and thereby contribute to cell wall sensing in roots (Dünser et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dünser et al., 2019

claim: The FER-RALF1-pectin signalling mechanism operates in an LRX-independent mode of action.
source: These findings suggest an LRX-independent mode of action in the FER-RALF1-pectin signalling mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the persistence of RALF1 activity in lrx quintuple mutants

claim: FER- and RALF-dependent roles of LRX proteins are distinct.
source: Our findings (this study and Dünser et al., 2019) pinpoint distinct FER- and RALF-dependent roles of LRX proteins.
evidence: Inferred from the differential requirements for LRX in different FER-dependent processes

claim: LRX8-RALF4-pectin interaction contributes to wall integrity and pollen tube expansion.
source: Considering that LRX8-RALF4-pectin interaction contributes to wall integrity and pollen tube expansion (Moussu et al., 2023), distinct modes of cell wall integrity control may be also in place in root cells and tip-growing pollen tubes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Moussu et al., 2023

claim: Distinct modes of cell wall integrity control may be in place in root cells and tip-growing pollen tubes.
source: Considering that LRX8-RALF4-pectin interaction contributes to wall integrity and pollen tube expansion (Moussu et al., 2023), distinct modes of cell wall integrity control may be also in place in root cells and tip-growing pollen tubes.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on comparison of different cell types

claim: Negatively charged, de-methylesterified pectin functions as a signalling scaffold for positively charged RALF peptides, which is crucial for its signalling via the FER receptor.
source: Based on our findings, we envision that negatively charged, de-methylesterified pectin could function as a signalling scaffold for positively charged RALF peptides, which seems crucial for its signalling via the FER receptor.
evidence: Speculative model based on the combined experimental findings

claim: The pectin sensing function of FER is physically separated from the RALF binding domain.
source: It needs to be seen how precisely the RALF binding to homogalacturonan affects its interaction with FER receptors. Here it is noteworthy that the pectin sensing function of FER is physically separated from the RALF binding domain (Gronnier et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gronnier et al., 2022

claim: High extracellular PME activity is expected to strongly acidify the apoplast.
source: The impact of de-methylesterified pectin on RALF signalling could also lead to self-emerging feedback properties because high extracellular PME activity is expected to strongly acidify the apoplast (Wolf et al., 2009)
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolf et al., 2009

claim: De-methylesterified pectin-induced activation of RALF peptides leads to apoplast alkalinisation.
source: The impact of de-methylesterified pectin on RALF signalling could also lead to self-emerging feedback properties because high extracellular PME activity is expected to strongly acidify the apoplast (Wolf et al., 2009), which in turn would be counteracted by the de-methylesterified pectin-induced activation of RALF peptides and its consequences on apoplast alkalinisation (Haruta et al., 2014; Barbez et al., 2017; this study).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haruta et al., 2014 and Barbez et al., 2017, and current study data

claim: Pectin functions in a PME-dependent manner as a tunable extracellular signalling scaffold.
source: In analogy, we propose that pectin functions in a PME-dependent manner as a tunable extracellular signalling scaffold.
evidence: Speculative model based on the combined findings

claim: Pectin is a heteropolysaccharide, primarily composed of galacturonic acid units, contributing to the mechanical strength and integrity of the cell wall.
source: Pectin is a heteropolysaccharide, primarily composed of galacturonic acid units, contributing to the mechanical strength and integrity of the cell wall.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about pectin structure and function

claim: Pectin (homogalacturonan) plays a vital role in growth control with an emerging role in signalling.
source: Pectin (homogalacturonan) plays a vital role in growth control with an emerging role in signalling (Wolf, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolf, 2022

claim: PMEs catalyse the removal of methyl groups from the initially esterified pectin, giving rise to negatively charged carboxylic acid groups.
source: In the cell wall, PMEs catalyse the removal of methyl groups from the initially esterified pectin, giving rise to negatively charged carboxylic acid groups and altering the interaction of pectin with various extracellular components (Peaucelle et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peaucelle et al., 2008

claim: RALF peptides are extracellular cysteine-rich plant peptide hormones.
source: Here, we address how the methylation status of pectin in the extracellular matrix contributes to the integration of RALFs, which are extracellular cysteine-rich plant peptide hormones.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about RALF peptides

claim: RALF peptides are involved in multiple physiological and developmental processes, ranging from organ and pollen tube growth to the modulation of immune responses.
source: RALF peptides are involved in multiple physiological and developmental processes, ranging from organ and pollen tube growth to the modulation of immune responses (Stegmann et al., 2017; Abarca et al., 2021; Mecchia et al., 2017; Geldner et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stegmann et al., 2017; Abarca et al., 2021; Mecchia et al., 2017; Geldner et al., 2009

claim: CrRLK1L are transmembrane proteins with an extracellular domain, consisting of two adjacent malectin-like domains, for RALF signal perception and a cytoplasmic kinase domain for intracellular signal transduction.
source: Catharanthus roseus receptor-like kinase 1-like (CrRLK1L) are transmembrane proteins with an extracellular domain, consisting of two adjacent malectin-like domains, for RALF signal perception and a cytoplasmic kinase domain for intracellular signal transduction (Escobar-Restrepo et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Escobar-Restrepo et al., 2007

claim: Feronia (FER) is currently the best characterized CrRLK1L.
source: Feronia (FER) is currently the best characterized CrRLK1L, contributing to the above-mentioned developmental programs as well as the integration of environmental cues (Feng et al., 2018; Gigli Bisceglia et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 2018 and Gigli Bisceglia et al., 2022

claim: RALF binding to FER modulates cell wall properties, ion fluxes, and enzymatic activities, thereby influencing cellular expansion rates.
source: On a cellular level, RALF binding to FER leads to rapid apoplastic (extracellular) alkalinisation (Haruta et al., 2014), which modulates cell wall properties, ion fluxes, and enzymatic activities, thereby influencing cellular expansion rates (Haruta et al., 2014; Barbez et al., 2017; Dünser et al., 2019; Dünser and Kleine-Vehn, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Haruta et al., 2014; Barbez et al., 2017; Dünser et al., 2019; Dünser and Kleine-Vehn, 2015

claim: CrRLK1Ls play a role in cell wall sensing.
source: Besides its role in apoplastic pH, CrRLK1Ls play a role in cell wall sensing (Hématy et al., 2007; Höfte, 2015; Shih et al., 2014)
